So, we end up where we began: where are we and where are we going? Thanks. Audience Q&A Aldy: So, I'll open with the first question, and then we'll take questions from the audience. Right before we started, I mentioned, Dan, that the title of your talk is one that could have been given about 20 years ago. There was a lot of talk about the nuclear power renaissance in the United States then - something that we worked on to some degree at the beginning of the Obama administration. But some things didn't come to pass, like a price on carbon. Some things did, like innovation driving down natural gas prices, and we didn't really realize that kind of nuclear power renaissance. One thing that looks different today, as you noted, is the potential interest on the demand side of these major corporations who need power for their data centers. Could you explore a little bit more what you think that potential could be and where there might be, as you noted, public-private partnerships that could actually create the kind of market necessary for us to really scale up commercial deployment of new nuclear power units in the United States? Poneman: Great question, Joe. A lot of the economics depends on scale. Anything you build just one of, that's why they call it first-of-a-kind cost. So, if these hyperscalers get together - and I think, frankly, it'd be well if there were some skinning down of the number of designs being supported, just in terms of market development - I think you have a chance of starting to drive down the cost by building up a supply chain and starting a repeated process. Even if they pursue different technologies, a lot of the things can translate from one to the other. For example, the steam turbine plant, it's the same for a lot of these folks. The need for skilled operators, it's the same for a lot of these folks. So, if we can start to build a whole industry around the advent of a huge demand gap to be filled and big balance sheets to fill it, then I think you can start the building blocks that can help do what is critical, which is to drive down the cost of the supply chain. And if you have a little assist from an NRC that now seems to be much more inclined to be helpful - and I don't mean, to be very clear, lax. Aldy: What does an assist look like from the NRC? Poneman: They need to, I think, be more efficient in the application of regulations. I think, like everyone else, they have to use AI. They have to use risk-based analysis, and they have to, I think, understand that their mission is - and the good news about the new mission statement is it says so - they need to be regulating the safety to enable the deployment. I think it's been a little bit imbalanced. So, I think those are the elements that can come together. Momentum is a real thing, Joe, and if we get that kind of workforce... I have spent a lot of time talking to organized labor. People are ready, but - and this is a sort of a sad footnote - I am told it would've been great if Vogtle 3 and 4 were followed by 5 and 6, but people do get other offers. So, pace matters. If this demand curve holds up, and so far, it seems to be, that promises enough demand that you start getting these things built. But we have to get on with it. One other thing I would say is there are different generations. So, when it comes to large plants, there's already a well-established regulatory predicate. There are approved designs. There are existing supply chains. There's existing fuel forms. Those are likelier to be easier to get going sooner, and I would not wish the promise of more advanced technologies to have us hold back on what we need to deploy today, because I think the supply chain can be sufficiently robust that it can support different generations, but the most important thing is to start. Aldy: Let me start with some questions from the audience now. Audience Member: Thank you, Dan, for this very insightful presentation. So, as you may know, Saudi Arabia and the United States have signed a nuclear cooperation deal just a couple of days ago. What would be the geopolitical implications of that, and will it change the slide that you had on the domino effect of the uranium risks? Poneman: I have not seen the details of that. In my time at the Department of Energy, as you may recall, I was the co-chair of the U.S.-Saudi energy dialogue. We talked about this a lot, and I remember Minister Naimi at the time said, "We have three great assets: oil, sun, and sand." So, they were leaning in those days into not just oil but actually solar. But I would say the following, if Saudi is to follow the example of the United Arab Emirates, it's a very good sign, and what do I mean by that? The UAE, around 2005 or 2006, realized they need a lot more baseload, and they came and explained to some Americans, "Look, we either have to do coal or nuclear, and we don't have infrastructure for either." They were already thinking about Masdar and their own commitments about CO2, so they favored nuclear. Once they made that decision, they took a series of steps to - if I put it crudely, they did it right. They had a very thoughtful internal policy development process that produced a white paper that became codified in a law that said, "We are not going to enrich uranium or reprocess plutonium, which would be a proliferation threat and make the region and the world nervous." They put in absolutely top-drawer safety regulators. They brought in the biggest contractors with the best technologies. So, they built these four plants at Barakah, and I've visited a couple times, and Barakah 2 was faster than Barakah 1. 3 was faster than 2, 4 was faster than 3, and they did it right. They showed a learning curve and now they get 25% of electricity [from those plants]. So, this could be the way of the future. Saudi is obviously the next major player in that region. I would say if the way this is fulfilled is consistent with the way the UAE was fulfilled, it could be a great thing not only for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, but for the region and beyond. Audience Member: Thank you, Dan. Thank you for your very insightful remarks.

How do you think we can balance between offering comprehensive build-own-operate packages and ensuring that such offers do not undermine the global nonproliferation norms, especially when China and Russia may not insist on the same standard? Thank you. Poneman: Yeah, great question. So, I think you have to divide it into two pieces, right? The sensitive part of commercial commerce is typically the fuel cycle, not the actual nuclear power reactor itself. It's the enriched uranium at the front end and potentially the separated plutonium at the back end. So, build-own-operate per se does not, I think, create novel challenges in terms of safeguards and that sort of thing, but what it does create in terms of risk is, as I quoted Ernie Moniz, "No export, no influence." Secondly, frankly, the sort of sclerotic view that maybe some U.S. exporters had about - I'm not going to do this or that business model. They say you have to meet your customer where are, and maybe there are build-own-operate options that might be attractive or viable, and we don't have to simply say, "Oh, we're not doing that.
